state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think Fido falling asleep is represented by the negative-sloping section of the graph? How does this interpretation align with what you know about distance-time graphs and the movement of objects?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, well I thought that because the line goes down, it means something bad is happening, like Fido stopping or sleeping? But now I'm not sure... does the line going down actually mean he's moving backwards towards his home instead?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: How does the direction of the line on the graph relate to Fido's movement in relation to his home? Think about the misconceptions we've discussed before, such as misinterpreting horizontal or negative-sloping lines on distance-time graphs.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so when the line goes down, that means the distance is getting smaller, so Fido must be moving back towards his home, yeah? But I'm still a bit confused about the horizontal bit in the middle - does that mean he's stopped moving, or is he still going somewhere?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the specific misconception about rest vs. movement through targeted questioning that prompts student reasoning, leading to visible improvement as the student correctly identifies that downward slopes mean returning home and asks appropriately about the horizontal section representing rest.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never provides direct answers, and prompts the student to reconsider their flawed reasoning about the graph's meaning, which is a textbook example of Socratic teaching.
